content: The policy of testing all blood donations for human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV-I/II) antibodies has been implemented in several countries. Seven countries have adopted selective testing, targeting either new donors or those who have not been previously tested. In Africa, one country conducts HTLV-I/II testing. In the Americas, 22 countries plus one additional country perform such testing. In the Eastern Mediterranean region, four countries plus one additional country test for HTLV-I/II. In Europe, eight countries plus three additional countries conduct testing. In the Western Pacific region, two countries plus two additional countries test for HTLV-I/II. Selective testing is practiced in some countries, such as the Netherlands, where all donations were tested until July 2013. Since then, testing has been limited to new donors prior to their first donation. Thirteen countries, including six in Africa, three in the Americas, three in the Western Pacific, and one in the Eastern Mediterranean, reported being unable to test 100% of collected blood for one or more of the four transfusion-transmissible infections (HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis) as required by national testing policies. Seven countries (three in the Americas, two in Africa, one in the Eastern Mediterranean, and one in the Western Pacific) reported being unable to test all donations for HIV. One country in the Western Pacific region reported not testing donated blood for HCV. Nine countries (three in Africa, three in the Americas, two in the Eastern Mediterranean, and one in the Western Pacific) reported being unable to test all donations for syphilis. Three European countries do not routinely test for syphilis due to changes in national policies. One country in Africa, three in the Eastern Mediterranean, two in the Americas, and one in the Western Pacific were unable to provide data on the coverage of one or more screening tests for the four key infectious markers (HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis). Tables 11–14 provide details on the coverage of laboratory screening for HIV-1/2, HBV, HCV, and syphilis by WHO region. The irregular supply of test kits is a significant barrier to achieving 100% screening coverage for the four key transfusion-transmitted infections. In 2013, 35 countries (20 in Africa, seven in the Americas, four in Africa, two in the Eastern Mediterranean, and one each in South-East Asia and the Western Pacific) reported stock-outs of test kits for transfusion-transmissible infections at the national or regional level during the reporting period. To ensure quality-assured blood screening, data were collected on the use of standard operating procedures and participation in external quality assessment programs. Reports from 137 countries indicated that 97% of blood donations were screened following basic quality-assured procedures. However, disparities exist, with 97% of donations in upper-middle-income countries, 81% in lower-middle-income countries, and 66% in low-income countries meeting these criteria. The prevalence of infection markers in blood donations is directly related to the safety of the blood supply. This prevalence impacts the residual risk of distributed blood products and the risk of errors in blood quarantine and release. The prevalence of infections in blood donations depends on the infection prevalence in the donor population and the effectiveness of donor recruitment and selection processes. Table 15 shows the proportion of blood donations with positive or reactive results for HIV, HBV, HCV, and syphilis by income group. Globally, the proportions vary significantly, with the lowest in developed countries and the highest in developing countries. In sub-Saharan Africa, data from selected countries show that a high prevalence of HIV in the general population does not necessarily translate to a high prevalence among blood donors. A blood collection system based on repeat and voluntary non-remunerated blood donors can significantly reduce the prevalence of HIV among recruited donors. In 2013, 8 million blood donations were discarded due to reactivity for markers of transfusion-transmissible infections. Other reasons for discarding blood included outdated stock and incomplete collection. Appropriate stock management is essential to minimize wastage due to expiry, particularly in low-income countries where stock levels are often low, and transfusions are arranged on an ad hoc basis. Significant differences exist in blood use patterns between high-, middle-, and low-income countries. In high-income countries, transfusions are primarily used for cardiovascular and transplant surgery, massive trauma, and therapy for malignancies. In contrast, in lowand middle-income countries, up to 67% of transfusions are for children under five years, followed by females aged 15–45 years. The use of whole blood versus blood components varies significantly by income group. In high-income countries, whole blood is rarely used, while in upper-middle-, lower-middle-, and low-income countries, 1%, 24%, and 85% of blood, respectively, is transfused as whole blood. As health systems develop, component therapy becomes increasingly important for clinical management. Platelets can be prepared from whole blood or through apheresis. Countries such as Belgium, China, Germany, Japan, and the United States primarily provide platelets through apheresis collection, while others rely on whole blood collection.
